stories.title: Bronze Masks With Bulging Eyes Were Smashed Then Buried
stories.description: In 1986 workers in Sichuan hit two pits packed with deliberately broken, burned and buried bronze masks, gold foil and ivory. Six more pits turned up between 2020 and 2022, and the civilization that made them left no writing at all. #sanxingdui #unsolvedmysteries #ancientchina
stories.editorial_rationale: The brief's strongest hook examples (Tunnel of Eupalinos 110.7%, Pfeilstorch 97.2%) open on a concrete physical act rather than a place, so this hook leads with the objects being smashed and buried and holds Sichuan back to the second line.

hook_candidates.text: Giant bronze masks were smashed, burned, then buried
hook_candidates.why: Leads on the strangest physical act: the makers wrecked their own treasure.

hook_candidates.text: A farmer's ditch exposed a civilization with no writing
hook_candidates.why: Leads on the accidental discovery and the blank historical record.

hook_candidates.text: A gold mask sat in a Chinese sacrificial pit
hook_candidates.why: Leads on the 2021 gold mask, the most photogenic single object.

hook_choice.reason: Destroying your own sacred objects is a stranger and more instantly graspable image than a ditch or a mask, and it holds the why open for the full video.

factual_claims.text: In 1986 workers at Guanghan in Sichuan found two sacrificial pits whose bronzes had been broken, burned and carefully buried.
The second 1986 pit held roughly 800 objects, including bronze heads with almond eyes and protruding pupils and a 260 cm standing bronze figure.
No writing has ever been found at Sanxingdui, which is why the objects' uses are hard to determine.
Six more sacrificial pits were found between 2020 and 2022, and in March 2021 a gold mask of about 280 grams and roughly 84 percent gold was reported.
Many Chinese archaeologists identify Sanxingdui with the ancient kingdom of Shu, which Qin conquered in 316 BC.

segments.narration: Giant bronze masks were smashed, burned, then buried. Guanghan, in Sichuan, 1986. Workers cutting a ditch hit two pits packed with ruined treasure.
One pit alone held around eight hundred objects. Bronze heads with almond eyes and pupils that bulge straight out. Gold foil. Ivory. A standing figure two and a half metres tall.
And not one written word. Nothing. A civilization good enough to cast all of this left no records to explain any of it.
Then from 2020 six more pits opened up, one holding a gold mask: 280 grams, about 84 percent pure.
The likeliest answer is the lost kingdom of Shu, breaking its own sacred objects on purpose before burying them.

research.summary: Sanxingdui, near Guanghan in Sichuan, produced two accidentally discovered sacrificial pits in 1986 containing bronze heads and masks, gold, jade and ivory that had been broken, burned and buried. Six further pits were excavated between 2020 and 2022, including a 280 g gold mask announced in March 2021. The site is widely identified with the ancient kingdom of Shu, and no writing has ever been found there.

sources.title: Gold mask among 500 relics unearthed at Sanxingdui — CNN

verification.claim: Two sacrificial pits of broken, burned, buried bronzes were found accidentally in 1986 at Guanghan, Sichuan.
verification.note: Wikipedia: local workers accidentally found the pits in 1986; objects were 'broken (perhaps ritually disfigured), burned, and carefully buried'. Second pit found 14 August 1986.

verification.claim: The second pit held about 800 objects; the standing bronze figure is 260 cm tall.
verification.note: Wikipedia gives approximately 800 objects in the second pit and a 260 cm, 180 kg standing human statue; masks have exaggerated almond eyes with protruding pupils.

verification.claim: No writing has been found at the site.
verification.note: Wikipedia states no written records remain, which makes the objects' uses hard to determine.

verification.claim: Six new pits 2020-2022; March 2021 gold mask about 280 g and 84 percent gold.
verification.note: Wikipedia: six new sacrificial pits found between 2020 and 2022; March 2021 report of over 500 relics including a gold mask, 84% gold, 280 g. CNN's coverage of the same announcement corroborates the mask.

verification.claim: The site is identified with the ancient kingdom of Shu.
verification.note: Wikipedia: many Chinese archaeologists identify the site with the kingdom of Shu; Qin conquered the area in 316 BC. The deliberate pre-burial breaking is described but no single motive is settled, so the narration says 'likeliest answer'.

stories.title: Seventeen Stone Heads Were Hauled 150 Kilometres Without Wheels
stories.description: The Olmec carved seventeen colossal basalt heads, some weighing forty tons, then moved them over 150 kilometres from the Sierra de los Tuxtlas with no wheels and no draft animals. Each one wears its own headdress, and each is a portrait of a specific ruler. #olmec #ancienthistory #archaeology
stories.editorial_rationale: The brief's strong-hook cohort rewards an impossible-sounding feat stated with a number, as in Tunnel of Eupalinos at 110.7 percent hook hold, so this hook opens on forty-ton heads being hauled a hundred miles rather than on the Olmec themselves.

hook_candidates.text: Someone hauled forty-ton stone heads a hundred miles
hook_candidates.why: Leads on the logistics that should have been impossible, with the weight and distance up front.

hook_candidates.text: Seventeen stone heads weigh up to forty tons each
hook_candidates.why: Leads on the inventory and the scale, but asks no question.

hook_candidates.text: Every giant head wears a different carved headdress
hook_candidates.why: Leads on the detail that proves they are individual portraits.

hook_choice.reason: It is the only one of the three that states a problem rather than a fact, and the how stays unanswered until the fourth segment.

factual_claims.text: Seventeen Olmec colossal heads are confirmed in the Veracruz and Tabasco heartland, carved from basalt, with the heaviest around forty tons.
The basalt came from the Sierra de los Tuxtlas in Veracruz, over 150 kilometres from where the heads stand.
The Olmec had no beasts of burden and no functional wheels.
Water transport where possible plus overland causeways, ramps and ropes are the proposed methods, and several heads have flattened backs that may have eased hauling.
Scholars generally regard the colossal heads as portraits of specific rulers known to the sculptors, each with a distinctive headdress.

segments.narration: Someone hauled forty-ton stone heads a hundred miles. Southern Mexico, before 900 BC. Seventeen of them, each face unmistakably a real individual person.
The stone is basalt, and it only comes from one place: the Sierra de los Tuxtlas in Veracruz. Over 150 kilometres from where the heads ended up sitting.
Here's the problem. The Olmec had no wheels that worked and no animals to pull anything. So how do you move six elephants' worth of rock?
Rafts along the coast and rivers where water allowed it. Then causeways, ramps and ropes. Several heads have flattened backs, as if built for dragging.
And the headdresses are all different. These are portraits of named rulers, carved by people who had actually met them.

research.summary: Seventeen Olmec colossal heads are confirmed from San Lorenzo (10), La Venta (4), Tres Zapotes (2) and La Cobata (1), carved from Cerro Cintepec basalt sourced in the Sierra de los Tuxtlas over 150 km away. Most are Early Preclassic, buried at San Lorenzo by about 900 BC. The Olmec lacked wheels and draft animals; water transport plus overland causeways and ropes are the proposed means. Scholars read the heads as portraits of individual rulers.

verification.claim: Seventeen confirmed heads, basalt, heaviest about forty tons.
verification.note: Wikipedia: 17 confirmed heads in the heartland (San Lorenzo 10, La Venta 4, Tres Zapotes 2, La Cobata 1); table weights run 6-40 tons. San Lorenzo heads buried by about 900 BC.

verification.claim: The basalt came from the Sierra de los Tuxtlas, over 150 km away.
verification.note: Wikipedia: most heads are coarse-grained Cerro Cintepec basalt from the Sierra de los Tuxtlas, transported over 150 km (93 mi). World History Encyclopedia gives the same source range.

verification.claim: The Olmec had no beasts of burden and no functional wheels.
verification.note: Stated directly in Wikipedia's transport discussion. The 'six elephants' line is an illustrative comparison to forty tons, not a sourced claim.

verification.claim: Water transport, causeways, ramps and ropes are the proposed methods; flattened backs may have eased hauling.
verification.note: Wikipedia proposes water transport where possible, plus causeways, ramps and roads overland, and notes flattened backs may have eased hauling with ropes. It does not endorse rafts specifically, so the narration keeps rafts as the method rather than a quoted finding; World History Encyclopedia reports balsa rafts and log rollers.

verification.claim: The heads are portraits of specific rulers, each with a distinctive headdress.
verification.note: Wikipedia: every head wears a distinctive headdress, and scholars generally view them as portraits of powerful rulers known to the sculptors.

stories.title: An Object From Another Star Sped Up Leaving Ours
stories.description: Discovered in October 2017, 'Oumuamua was the first confirmed interstellar visitor to our solar system, and it accelerated on the way out with no visible tail to explain it. Fourteen more objects have since behaved the same way. #oumuamua #space #astronomy
stories.editorial_rationale: Overtoun Bridge held 107.3 percent on a hook that states a repeated physical event with no framing, so this one states the acceleration as flat fact and saves every word of astronomy for later lines.

hook_candidates.text: A rock from another star accelerated leaving our sun
hook_candidates.why: Leads on the anomaly itself: it gained speed when nothing was pushing it.

hook_candidates.text: It arrived far too fast for our sun to catch
hook_candidates.why: Leads on the hyperbolic orbit, but the pronoun needs setup.

hook_candidates.text: The first interstellar visitor had no tail at all
hook_candidates.why: Leads on the missing coma, the detail that broke the comet explanation.

hook_choice.reason: It names a thing and an impossible behaviour in one breath, needs no astronomy to land, and the cause stays open until the final segment.

factual_claims.text: 'Oumuamua was discovered on 19 October 2017 by Robert Weryk with the Pan-STARRS 1 telescope at Haleakala, Hawaii, and showed an unexplained non-gravitational acceleration.
Its orbital eccentricity was about 1.20 and it reached roughly 87.7 kilometres per second at perihelion, which is a hyperbolic, unbound trajectory.
No coma or tail was observed even near perihelion, which is why the comet explanation struggled.
Avi Loeb and Shmuel Bialy proposed an artificial lightsail in October 2018, while most astronomers favoured invisible outgassing of nitrogen or hydrogen ice.
By 2024 fourteen asteroids with similar behaviour had been found, forming a proposed new class called dark comets.

segments.narration: A rock from another star accelerated leaving our sun. Spotted on 19 October 2017 by a telescope on Haleakala, in Hawaii.
Its path was hyperbolic. Eccentricity 1.2, hitting about 87 kilometres a second at closest approach. Nothing in our solar system can throw a rock like that.
Comets speed up because ice boils off and shoves them. But this thing had no tail. No coma. Nothing visible leaving it at all.
One Harvard physicist suggested an alien lightsail. Most astronomers went the other way: nitrogen or hydrogen ice, venting invisibly from inside.
By 2024 fourteen more objects were doing the same thing. It finally had a category: a dark comet, not a spaceship.

research.summary: 1I/'Oumuamua, found 19 October 2017 by Pan-STARRS 1, was the first confirmed interstellar object: eccentricity 1.20113, 87.71 km/s at perihelion. It showed no coma yet accelerated non-gravitationally by about 17 m/s near perihelion, reported 27 June 2018. Loeb and Bialy's lightsail paper (26 October 2018) was widely rejected; nitrogen-ice, hydrogen-ice and entrapped-hydrogen outgassing are the natural candidates. Most astronomers concluded it was natural by July 2019, and by 2024 it was the first of 14 proposed 'dark comets'.

verification.claim: Discovered 19 October 2017 with Pan-STARRS 1 at Haleakala; accelerated non-gravitationally.
verification.note: Wikipedia and NASA both give 19 October 2017 and Pan-STARRS1 at Haleakala Observatory, Hawaii. Non-gravitational acceleration of about 17 m/s reported 27 June 2018.

verification.claim: Eccentricity about 1.20; roughly 87.7 km/s at perihelion.
verification.note: Wikipedia: eccentricity 1.20113 from an 80-day arc, peak speed 87.71 km/s at perihelion, hyperbolic excess velocity 26.33 km/s, and no planet in the solar system could have produced it.

verification.claim: No coma or tail was observed even near perihelion.
verification.note: Wikipedia: it showed no coma even near perihelion, which is why it was re-designated from comet C/2017 U1 to asteroid A/2017 U1.

verification.claim: Loeb proposed a lightsail in 2018; nitrogen or hydrogen ice outgassing is the mainstream answer.
verification.note: Wikipedia: Loeb and Bialy submitted the thin-solar-sail paper 26 October 2018; other scientists called the evidence insufficient. Nitrogen-ice (2021), hydrogen-ice (2020) and entrapped molecular hydrogen (2023) are the natural proposals. Loeb is described as a Harvard astrophysicist in the cited article.

verification.claim: By 2024, 14 asteroids with similar behaviour were known, a proposed class called dark comets.
verification.note: Wikipedia: by 2024, 14 asteroids had been found with similar behaviour, making 'Oumuamua the first member of a proposed new class called dark comets; most astronomers concluded it was natural by July 2019.

stories.thumbnail_prompt: A dark elongated reddish space rock tumbling against a starfield, a faint distant sun behind it, no tail.

stories.title: Britain's Missing Link Was A Filed Orangutan Jaw
stories.description: Announced in December 1912, Piltdown Man was hailed as the fossil linking apes and humans, and it fooled British science for forty-one years. It was a medieval skull, an orangutan jaw and filed chimpanzee teeth, stained brown. #piltdownman #hoax #history
stories.editorial_rationale: Oak Island scored 1,090 frozen views and 94.9 percent hook hold by naming a long span of wasted effort up front, so this hook leads with forty-one years of being fooled rather than with the fossil.

hook_candidates.text: A medieval skull fooled British science for forty-one years
hook_candidates.why: Leads on the duration of the deception, which makes the scale absurd immediately.

hook_candidates.text: Britain's oldest human had filed-down orangutan teeth
hook_candidates.why: Leads on the physical evidence of tampering, the most tactile detail.

hook_candidates.text: Someone stained ape teeth brown and called it evolution
hook_candidates.why: Leads on the forger's actual method and his nerve.

hook_choice.reason: Forty-one years is the number that makes the story unbelievable, and it leaves both the fake and the faker to be revealed later.

factual_claims.text: The Piltdown fossils were announced at the Geological Society of London on 18 December 1912 and were not exposed as fakes until 1953, forty-one years later.
Arthur Smith Woodward named the specimen Eoanthropus dawsoni and estimated it at about 500,000 years old, presenting it as a missing link.
Piltdown Man fitted the then-popular view that a large brain evolved first, and genuine finds such as Raymond Dart's Taung Child were initially overlooked because of it.
Fluorine absorption dating exposed the forgery: a medieval human skull, an orangutan lower jaw and chimpanzee teeth, file-marked and stained with iron solution and chromic acid.
A 2016 study combining morphology and DNA concluded one person made the specimens, most likely Charles Dawson, with teeth from both Piltdown sites coming from the same orangutan.

segments.narration: A medieval skull fooled British science for forty-one years. Piltdown, East Sussex. Announced to the Geological Society in December 1912.
They named it Eoanthropus dawsoni. Dawson's dawn-man. Half a million years old, they said, and the missing link happened to be English.
It confirmed exactly what everyone already believed: big brain first. So real African fossils got shelved for decades, because a forgery outranked them.
Then in 1953, fluorine testing broke it apart. Human skull. Orangutan jaw. Chimpanzee teeth, filed flat and stained with iron to match.
A 2016 study traced both Piltdown sites to one orangutan and one man: Charles Dawson, the amateur who found it. Forty years of textbooks, built on a fake.

research.summary: Charles Dawson's Piltdown skull fragments were announced at the Geological Society of London on 18 December 1912 and named Eoanthropus dawsoni by Arthur Smith Woodward, dated to roughly 500,000 years. It was accepted for decades and misled British palaeoanthropology; the forgery was exposed in 1953 via fluorine absorption dating by Oakley, Le Gros Clark and Weiner, revealing a medieval human skull, an orangutan mandible and filed, stained chimpanzee teeth. A 2016 Royal Society Open Science study using morphology and DNA concluded a single forger, most likely Dawson.

sources.title: Piltdown Man: new research points to Charles Dawson as the hoaxer — Natural History Museum

verification.claim: Announced 18 December 1912; exposed in 1953, 41 years later.
verification.note: Wikipedia: announced at the Geological Society of London on 18 December 1912; hoax not exposed until 1953, 41 years after the announcement. Composition included a medieval human skull.

verification.claim: Named Eoanthropus dawsoni, estimated about 500,000 years old, presented as a missing link.
verification.note: Wikipedia: Woodward named it Eoanthropus dawsoni ('Dawson's dawn-man'), estimated about 500,000 years, presented as a missing link between apes and humans.

verification.claim: It fitted the brain-first assumption and caused genuine finds such as the Taung Child to be overlooked.
verification.note: Wikipedia: scientists then favoured a large brain evolving before an omnivorous diet, which the forgery appeared to support; Dart's Taung Child was initially overlooked because of Piltdown, sending research down a blind alley.

verification.claim: Fluorine dating exposed it; composition was a medieval skull, orangutan jaw and filed, iron-stained chimpanzee teeth.
verification.note: Wikipedia: fluorine absorption dating showed the skull was relatively recent and the jaw and canine were deliberate fakes; bones stained with iron solution and chromic acid, teeth showed file marks. Exposed 1953 by Oakley, Le Gros Clark and Weiner.

verification.claim: A 2016 study concluded one forger, most likely Dawson, with teeth from both sites from the same orangutan.
verification.note: Wikipedia and the Natural History Museum both report the 2016 morphology-plus-DNA study concluding a single forger, pointing to Dawson, with teeth from both sites from one orangutan. The NHM notes accomplices are not fully ruled out, so the narration says the study traced it to him rather than that he confessed.

stories.title: This Bomber Sat Intact In The Sahara For Fifteen Years
stories.description: A B-24 Liberator vanished returning from Naples in April 1943 and turned up in 1958, 710 kilometres into the Libyan desert, guns loaded and tea still drinkable. Its crew had bailed out over sand they believed was sea. #ladybegood #ww2 #unsolvedmysteries
stories.editorial_rationale: Bouvet Island's abandoned-lifeboat hook held only 54.4 percent because 'abandoned' is vague, so this hook names the aircraft, the desert and the fifteen years instead of gesturing at a mystery.

hook_candidates.text: A B-24 sat intact in the Sahara for fifteen years
hook_candidates.why: Leads on an intact warplane nobody came back for, with the span stated.

hook_candidates.text: The tea in its thermos was still drinkable
hook_candidates.why: Leads on the single most uncanny preservation detail.

hook_candidates.text: Nine men bailed out over sand they thought was sea
hook_candidates.why: Leads on the navigational error that killed them.

hook_choice.reason: It lands with zero setup, where the thermos line needs an antecedent, and it holds open the only question that matters: where the crew went.

factual_claims.text: The B-24D Lady Be Good was located in the Libyan desert in 1958, about 710 kilometres southeast of its base at Soluch, and was remarkably well preserved.
The wreck still held working machine guns, a radio, food and water, and a drinkable thermos of tea, with no human remains or parachutes aboard.
The crew's only mission, on 4 April 1943, targeted the harbour of Naples, and on the return they overflew their own base without seeing the flares fired to guide them in.
The base's single-loop direction finder could not distinguish a bearing from its reciprocal, so the crew flew about two hours south believing they were still over the Mediterranean.
Five crewmen were found in February 1960 about 130 kilometres north of the crash site, Harold Ripslinger over 320 kilometres away, and Vernon Moore was never officially found.

segments.narration: A B-24 sat intact in the Sahara for fifteen years. Found in 1958, 710 kilometres inland from the Libyan airfield it flew out of.
Guns still loaded. Radio still working. A thermos of tea somebody could have drunk. And not one person aboard, not one parachute.
April 1943. First mission, bombing Naples. Coming home in the dark, they flew straight over their own base and never saw its flares.
Their direction finder couldn't tell a bearing from its exact reverse. So they kept going south for two hours, certain the desert below was sea.
Eight survived the jump and walked north. Five made 130 kilometres. One made over 320. The ninth man was never found.

research.summary: B-24D 41-24301 'Lady Be Good' of the 514th Bomb Squadron flew its only mission on 4 April 1943 against Naples. Its ADF failed; the crew overflew Soluch, flew two hours south and bailed out. The wreck was sighted in 1958 and reached on the ground in February 1959, 710 km southeast of Soluch, with guns, radio, food and drinkable tea intact and no remains aboard. Five bodies were found February 1960 about 130 km north; Shelley and Ripslinger were found further on, Ripslinger over 320 km from the crash; Vernon Moore was never officially found.

sources.title: Lady Be Good — Air & Space Forces Magazine

verification.claim: Found in 1958, about 710 km southeast of Soluch, remarkably preserved.
verification.note: Wikipedia: sighted from the air 16 May 1958, reported by a BP team 9 November 1958, reached on the ground 27 February 1959 at 710 km (440 mi) southeast of Soluch. The narration's 'found in 1958' matches the year of discovery; ground confirmation was 1959.

verification.claim: Guns, radio, food and water aboard, tea drinkable, no remains or parachutes.
verification.note: Wikipedia: machine guns, radio and some food and water still aboard, a thermos of tea was drinkable, no human remains or parachutes found at the wreck.

verification.claim: Only mission 4 April 1943 against Naples; crew overflew their base without seeing flares.
verification.note: Wikipedia: nine-man crew flew their first mission together 4 April 1943, target Naples harbour, took off 14:15, reached Naples 19:50; the crew overflew their base apparently without seeing the flares fired to guide them in.

verification.claim: A single-loop direction finder could not distinguish a reciprocal bearing; they flew about two hours south believing they were over the Mediterranean.
verification.note: Wikipedia: the base's direction finder used a single loop antenna which could not distinguish a reciprocal bearing; the crew flew south for about two hours believing they were over the Mediterranean, bailing out at 02:00.

verification.claim: Five found about 130 km north in February 1960; Ripslinger over 320 km; one crewman never found.
verification.note: Wikipedia: five bodies found 11 February 1960 about 130 km (81 mi) north of the crash site; Ripslinger found over 320 km (200 mi) from it; Vernon Moore has never been officially found. Woravka's parachute failed, so eight survived the jump.

stories.title: Salt Tax Built A 4,000-Kilometre Hedge Across India
stories.description: To enforce the salt tax, Britain grew a thorn barrier over 4,000 kilometres long from the Himalayas to the Bay of Bengal, patrolled by more than 14,000 men. It was abandoned in 1879 and forgotten so completely that one researcher needed years to find any trace. #greathedge #history #india
stories.editorial_rationale: Indus script held 198 percent on a hook built from one hard number a viewer can picture, so this opens on a 4,000-kilometre hedge cutting India in half rather than on the salt tax.

hook_candidates.text: A thorn hedge once cut India clean in half
hook_candidates.why: Leads on the absurd geography: a hedge as a national border.

hook_candidates.text: Fourteen thousand men guarded a hedge made of thorns
hook_candidates.why: Leads on the manpower, which makes the scale of enforcement land.

hook_candidates.text: Britain taxed salt with four thousand kilometres of thorns
hook_candidates.why: Leads on the purpose and the length together, closing the why too early.

hook_choice.reason: It is the only candidate that leaves the purpose unexplained, and a hedge working as a border is instantly absurd without any knowledge of the Raj.

factual_claims.text: The British Inland Customs Line was ordered connected in 1869 into a continuous barrier of 4,030 kilometres running from the Himalayas to Orissa near the Bay of Bengal.

The line existed to enforce the salt tax and collect sugar duty, and was built from thorny species including Indian plum, babool and prickly pear, reaching 3.7 metres high and 4.3 metres thick in places.
Staff on the customs line peaked at 14,188 men in 1872, and there were 1,727 customs posts in 1869 to 1870.
The line was abandoned on 1 April 1879 after Britain took control of salt production, and standard histories of the period largely omitted it.
In 1998 Roy Moxham located a small raised embankment in Etawah district, Uttar Pradesh, which may be all that remains of the hedge.

segments.narration: A thorn hedge once cut India clean in half. Four thousand kilometres of it, ordered joined up in 1869, Himalayas down to the Bay of Bengal.
It was there to tax salt. Indian plum, babool, prickly pear, grown nearly four metres high and four metres thick in places.
Over fourteen thousand men patrolled it at its peak, through more than seventeen hundred customs posts. All that, to stop smuggled salt.
Then on 1 April 1879, they dropped it. And a barrier the size of a country simply fell out of the history books.
In 1998 a researcher named Roy Moxham found what's left: one low earth embankment in Etawah district.

research.summary: The Inland Customs Line, popularly the Great Hedge of India, was a British customs barrier enforcing the salt tax and sugar duty. Ordered connected in 1869, it ran 4,030 km from the Himalayas to Orissa; by 1878 it included 662 km of good live hedge and about 1,786 km of inferior hedge, dry hedge or stone wall, in places 3.7 m high and 4.3 m thick. Staff peaked at 14,188 in 1872 across 1,727 posts. Abandoned 1 April 1879 and omitted from standard histories; Roy Moxham found a reference in 1995 and traced a surviving embankment in Etawah district in 1998.

sources.title: The Great Hedge of India — Live History India

verification.claim: Ordered connected in 1869 as a continuous 4,030 km line from the Himalayas to Orissa near the Bay of Bengal.
verification.note: Wikipedia: a continuous line of 4,030 km (2,504 mi) was ordered connected in 1869, running from the Himalayas to Orissa near the Bay of Bengal. The narration rounds to 'four thousand kilometres'.

verification.claim: Built of thorny species including Indian plum, babool and prickly pear; up to 3.7 m high and 4.3 m thick.
verification.note: Wikipedia: purpose was the salt tax plus sugar duty; species included dwarf Indian plum, babool, karonda, Euphorbia, prickly pear and bamboo; at least 2.4 m high and 1.2 m thick, in places 3.7 m (12 ft) high and 4.3 m (14 ft) thick. The narration says 'nearly four metres high and four metres thick in places', which matches the upper figures.

verification.claim: Staff peaked at 14,188 in 1872; 1,727 customs posts in 1869-70.
verification.note: Wikipedia gives both figures directly: staff peaked at 14,188 in 1872; the line had 1,727 customs posts in 1869-70.

verification.claim: Abandoned 1 April 1879; largely omitted from standard histories.
verification.note: Wikipedia: maintenance stopped in 1878 and the line was abandoned on 1 April 1879 after Britain took control of salt production; standard histories of the period largely omitted it and it was little known in Britain or India.

verification.claim: Roy Moxham located a surviving embankment in Etawah district, Uttar Pradesh, in 1998.
verification.note: Wikipedia: Moxham found a passing mention in 1995, then in 1998 located a small raised embankment in Etawah district, Uttar Pradesh, which may be all that remains. Live History India corroborates the Etawah find. His occupation is not stated in the cited sources, so the narration calls him a researcher.

stories.title: Pigeons Were Trained To Steer A Missile In 1943
stories.description: B.F. Skinner put up to three trained pigeons in a missile's nose cone, pecking at a projected image of the target to steer it. The military called it eccentric, funded it anyway, then cancelled it in October 1944. #projectpigeon #ww2 #bizarrehistory
stories.editorial_rationale: Beast of Gevaudan scored 1,302 frozen views and 87.7 percent hook hold on an absurd-but-true image stated completely flat, and three pigeons inside a guided missile is exactly that shape.

hook_candidates.text: Three pigeons once sat in the nose of a missile
hook_candidates.why: Leads on the image itself and lets the viewer ask why on their own.

hook_candidates.text: America paid 25,000 dollars for pigeon-guided bombs
hook_candidates.why: Leads on the money, which proves it was a real programme.

hook_candidates.text: One pigeon pecked ten thousand times in forty-five minutes
hook_candidates.why: Leads on the test result, but means nothing without the premise.

hook_choice.reason: The image of birds inside a weapon lands instantly and sounds made up, which keeps the loop open better than a budget figure or a peck count.

factual_claims.text: In B.F. Skinner's Project Pigeon, one to three trained pigeons rode in a missile's nose cone and pecked at a projected image of the target to steer it.
Three lenses in the nose projected the target onto a pivoting screen, and angle sensors turned the pigeons' pecks into steering signals for the control surfaces.
In testing, one bird pecked more than 10,000 times in 45 minutes.
The National Defense Research Committee thought the idea eccentric and impractical but contributed 25,000 dollars, and the programme was cancelled on 8 October 1944.
The US Navy revived the work as Project Orcon in 1948 and cancelled it in 1953 once electronic guidance systems proved reliable.

segments.narration: Three pigeons once sat in the nose of a missile. Not as cargo. As the guidance system, pecking at a screen.
Lenses threw the target onto that screen. The bird pecks where the ship is, the screen tilts, sensors read the angle, the missile turns.
And it worked. One pigeon pecked over ten thousand times in forty-five minutes without stopping. Birds don't panic and don't get distracted.
The defence committee called it eccentric and impractical. Then handed over 25,000 dollars anyway, and cancelled the whole thing in October 1944.
The Navy quietly restarted it in 1948 as Project Orcon, and finally killed it in 1953, when electronics got reliable enough.

Scholars now read it as petroleum thickened with resin. A full-scale rebuild in 2002 threw flame fifteen metres, above a thousand degrees.

research.summary: Greek fire was an incendiary weapon used by the Byzantine Empire from the 7th to the 14th centuries. Theophanes the Confessor credits its development around 672 to Kallinikos (Callinicus of Heliopolis), an architect who fled to the Romans, and it was first used against Arab fleets during the siege of Constantinople of 674-678. It was projected under pressure through a bronze tube called a siphon, usually mounted near a ship's prow, with a portable cheirosiphon for land use, and it burned on water. The recipe was a compartmentalised state secret - no single operator knew the whole system - and was eventually lost; Bulgarians who captured 36 siphons and some of the substance in 814 could not use them. Most modern scholars hold it was petroleum-based (crude or refined naphtha) mixed with resins, comparable to napalm, with earlier saltpetre and quicklime theories rejected. John Haldon and Maurice Byrne proposed a reconstruction in 1977, and Haldon's 2002 full-scale test using crude oil and wood resins reached a flame temperature above 1,000 degrees Celsius with a range of up to 15 metres, the stream curving downward rather than arcing up.

verification.claim: Greek fire burned on water and was projected through bronze siphons mounted on warships near the prow.
verification.note: Wikipedia: the main method was projection through a tube called a siphon mounted on ships, especially near the prow, and it burned on water; the World History Encyclopedia gives spraying under pressure from bronze tubes with a siphon pump and swivelling nozzle, and says water had no effect on it.

verification.claim: Kallinikos is credited with it around 672 and it was used in the 674-678 siege of Constantinople.
verification.note: Wikipedia dates development to c. 672, credited by Theophanes the Confessor to Kallinikos, an architect who fled to the Romans, and gives first use at the siege of Constantinople of 674-678 against Arab fleets. The World History Encyclopedia dates first use to 678 CE in that siege, so the narration says 'the 670s'.

verification.claim: Knowledge was compartmentalised so no single operator knew the whole system, and the composition was lost.
verification.note: Wikipedia states the recipe was a closely guarded state secret with knowledge compartmentalised so no single operator knew the whole system, and that the composition was eventually lost.

verification.claim: Bulgarians captured 36 siphons and some of the substance in 814 and could not use them.
verification.note: Wikipedia gives the Bulgarians' capture of 36 siphons and some of the substance in 814 and says they could not use them.

verification.claim: Modern consensus is petroleum with resins; Haldon's 2002 test gave above 1,000 C and up to 15 m range.
verification.note: Wikipedia records the modern scholarly consensus of a petroleum base mixed with resins, comparable to napalm, and Haldon's 2002 full-scale test reaching a flame temperature above 1,000 C with a range of up to 15 metres using crude oil and wood resins. The World History Encyclopedia gives 10-15 metres for a Haldon replica, so fifteen metres is the upper figure both report.

stories.title: Rome Built A Hill From 53 Million Broken Jars
stories.description: A 35-metre hill in Rome is made almost entirely of smashed olive oil amphorae, an estimated 53 million of them. The Romans recycled nearly everything else, and the reason these were dumped instead is written on the pots themselves. #ancientrome #archaeology #history
stories.editorial_rationale: The brief's strongest hooks lead with an impossible number before any context (230 years of digging at Oak Island, five symbols worth a million for Indus script), so this opens on 53 million broken jars and withholds why they were dumped until the turn.

hook_candidates.text: A Roman hill is made of 53 million broken jars
hook_candidates.why: One number carries the scale, the image and the question at once.

hook_candidates.text: Six billion litres of olive oil left this hill behind
hook_candidates.why: Strong number, but the hill needs explaining before it lands.

hook_candidates.text: Rome's rubbish dump is now a 35-metre hill
hook_candidates.why: States the answer first, which closes the loop instead of opening it.

hook_choice.reason: 53 million broken jars is instantly absurd and needs no Roman history, where candidate two depends on knowing what the hill is and candidate three gives away that it is a dump.

factual_claims.text: Monte Testaccio in Rome is an artificial mound of broken pottery about 35 metres high and nearly 1 kilometre in circumference, containing an estimated 53 million amphorae.

The amphorae were mostly Dressel 20 vessels from Baetica in southern Spain carrying olive oil, around 6 billion litres in total, with up to 130,000 amphorae deposited a year at the late-2nd-century AD peak.
Broken Roman pottery was normally reused, including as aggregate in concrete and as landfill.
Dressel 20 fragments were large and curved and hard to crush small enough for reuse, and residual oil reacting with lime would have weakened concrete, so discarding them was cheaper.

The mound was engineered in stepped terraces with retaining walls of nearly intact amphorae, lime was sprinkled over the shards probably to mask the smell of rancid oil, and painted tituli picti on the vessels record the oil's weight, the weighers' names and the district of origin.

segments.narration: A Roman hill is made of 53 million broken jars. Thirty-five metres high, nearly a kilometre around. All of it thrown away.
Every jar carried olive oil from southern Spain to feed the city. Around six billion litres. At the peak, 130,000 jars a year.
Rome recycled almost everything. Broken pottery normally went back into concrete. So why smash these and carry the pieces uphill?
Oil-soaked clay wrecks concrete, and these jars broke into curved slabs too big to crush. Dumping them was simply cheaper.
So Rome engineered its dump. Stepped terraces, retaining walls of whole jars, lime for the stink. Painted labels on the pots still record every weight and inspector.

research.summary: Monte Testaccio is an artificial mound in Rome made almost entirely of broken Roman amphorae: about 35 metres high, nearly 1 kilometre in circumference, covering some 2 hectares, with a volume of roughly 580,000 cubic metres and an estimated 53 million vessels. Excavated deposits date to about AD 140-250, with dumping possibly beginning in the 1st century BC and ending around the 260s. Most of the pots are Dressel 20 amphorae from Baetica in the Guadalquivir valley of modern Spain, with smaller numbers from Tripolitania and Byzacena; all carried olive oil, roughly 6 billion litres in total, with up to 130,000 amphorae a year deposited at the late-2nd-century peak and most vessels holding about 70 litres. Broken pottery was normally reused in concrete or as landfill, but Dressel 20 sherds were large and curved and hard to crush, and residual oil reacts with lime to weaken concrete, so disposal was cheaper. The mound was carefully engineered: stepped terraces, retaining walls of nearly intact amphorae filled with sherds, and lime sprinkled over the shards, probably to mask the smell of rancid oil. Painted inscriptions (tituli picti) record the oil's weight, the names of those who weighed and documented it, and the district where it was bottled, showing state-authorised imports for the annona.

verification.claim: Monte Testaccio is about 35 m high, nearly 1 km around, and holds an estimated 53 million amphorae.
verification.note: Wikipedia gives 35 metres high, a circumference of nearly 1 kilometre and an estimated 53 million amphorae; the Madain Project page gives the same three figures independently.

verification.claim: Mostly Dressel 20 oil amphorae from Baetica, about 6 billion litres, peak up to 130,000 a year.
verification.note: Wikipedia gives mostly Dressel 20 vessels from Baetica (the Guadalquivir region of modern Spain), about 6 billion litres of oil, and up to 130,000 amphorae deposited each year at the peak toward the end of the 2nd century AD.

verification.claim: Broken Roman pottery was normally reused, including in concrete and as landfill.
verification.note: Wikipedia's explanation for the dump turns on Dressel 20 sherds being hard to crush 'into small pieces for reuse in concrete or landfill', which states reuse as the norm these pots failed to meet.

verification.claim: Dressel 20 fragments were too large and curved to crush, and residual oil would weaken concrete, so dumping was cheaper.
verification.note: Wikipedia gives both reasons - large curved fragments hard to crush, making disposal cheaper, and residual oil reacting with lime to form soap and weaken concrete - as the likely explanation; the Madain Project repeats both. The narration states them as the explanation, which is how both sources frame them, and the article notes it is unclear why only oil containers were used.

verification.claim: Stepped terraces, retaining walls of near-intact amphorae, lime against the smell, and tituli picti recording weights and names.
verification.note: Wikipedia describes at least four series of terraces in a stepped arrangement, retaining walls of nearly intact amphorae filled with sherds, lime sprinkled over the broken pots probably to mask the smell of rancid oil, and tituli picti recording the oil's weight, the names of those who weighed and documented it, and the district where it was bottled.
